The irons were hammered shut at dusk, the blacksmith’s own shackles fastened by a jailer who laughed at the irony.  Korrin, tongue long ago traded for silence, ears sealed by the plague’s black rot, felt the weight of the chain jerk him against the merchant—Arlowe of the hundred silver promises and thousand broken ones.  The colony’s palisade stank of pitch and vomit; beyond it, the healthy world pretended they were already ghosts.

Arlowe coughed, delicate even in sickness.  “Congratulations, mute.  We’re married.”  His voice was a honeyed rasp, the same timbre that once sold relic bones to bishops and duke’s wives their own husbands’ secrets.

Korrin answered with a glare hot enough to temper steel.  He lifted his palms, calloused maps of a lifetime at the forge, and signed: We leave tonight.

Arlowe read the shapes with scandal-bright eyes.  “Leave?  The guards have pikes, the river has leeches, and the plague has us.”  He rattled their shared chain.  “Unless you plan to file through this with courtesy?”

Korrin shook his head, pointed to the lantern where velvet moths battered their wings against hot glass.  He pinched a pellet of tallow mixed with his own blood—drawn earlier with a smuggled awl—then pressed it between thumb and forefinger until the grease turned crimson.  A moth landed, sipped, and fluttered drunkenly toward the night beyond the fence.

Arlowe’s laugh cracked.  “You’re feeding lies to bugs?  Even if wings could carry gossip, who’d listen?”

Korrin signed: The world listens to you.  Give them something worth hearing.

The merchant’s smile faltered, replaced by the predator’s grin that once emptied coffers.  He bit his lip, drew blood, and mixed it with the tallow.  Whispering, he shaped a lie so obscene it felt sacred: the Duke’s heir had pawned his war-chest to buy silken garters for the bishop’s stable-boy, and the plague cure was locked in that very coffer, gold-leafed and waiting.

The moths drank, wings blotched like confessionals.  One by one they spiraled over the palisade, carrying whispers to taverns, brothels, confessionals, until the city’s bells rang at midnight with demands to open the colony and retrieve the heir’s imaginary cure.

Inside, fever bit their bones.  Korrin’s hammered arms shook; Arlowe spat pink.  When the riot started, they crawled through a postern left unguarded by a guard who’d gone to join the looting.  Rain slicked their chain as they stumbled into the forest, following moth-shadows cast by torches behind them.

At dawn they collapsed beside a cold anvil of stone.  Arlowe, lips blue, whispered, “We’re free, mute.  Now demand your price—my tongue, my life, my silence?”

Korrin pressed two fingers to the merchant’s mouth, gentle as setting a rivet.  He signed: No more lies.  Only iron.

From his pocket he drew a tiny key he had forged in secret weeks ago, filing it against his own chains each night while the world wasn’t listening.  It clicked, the manacle falling open like a finished story.

Arlowe stared at the unbroken circle of iron, then at the blacksmith walking away barefoot, hammer slung across shoulder.  For once, the scandal-tongued man had no words.  Above them, weary moths drifted sunward, wings washed clean by rain, carrying nothing but ordinary morning light.
